answers.answer: It splits the document sequentially into fixed-size chunks, using a predefined or user-specified number of sentences per chunk, so the boundary comes from a counter rather than from the content. Because it needs no model and no boundary detection, it is the cheap baseline, and any costlier strategy has to show a gain over it.
accept: splits sequentially by a set length or a set number of sentences per chunk
the boundary is decided by a counter, not by the text
it costs almost nothing to run, so more expensive strategies are judged by whether they beat it

answers.answer: Their datasets were built by stitching documents together. As document length increased, fewer documents were stitched into each example, so topic diversity dropped, and with less topic diversity there was less for a breakpoint-based chunker to detect. Its advantage diminished accordingly.
accept: longer documents meant fewer documents stitched together per example
less topic diversity leaves the semantic chunker less to gain over a length-based split

answers.answer: Overlap repeats text across a boundary so a passage cut by the split still appears whole in one chunk. It pays for that with duplicated tokens: reducing overlap improves IoU scores because that metric penalises redundant information. Chroma evaluated the published OpenAI Assistants default of 800-token chunks with 400 tokens of overlap, assuming TokenTextSplitter, and measured slightly below-average recall with the lowest scores across every other metric.
accept: overlap preserves continuity across a boundary so a split passage still appears intact somewhere
it introduces redundant duplicated text, and reducing overlap improves IoU because that metric penalises redundancy
the 800 with 400 overlap setting measured slightly below-average recall and the lowest scores on the other metrics

answers.answer: Recall at 10 chunks counts units of different size, so the 800-token run is scored after retrieving four times as much text as the 200-token run and gets credit for volume rather than for placing boundaries well. Token-level scoring counts which tokens of the relevant passage were retrieved and which irrelevant tokens came with them, which puts chunkers of different sizes on one scale.
accept: a chunk is not a fixed amount of text, so ten chunks means very different amounts of text in the two runs
the larger setting is advantaged by retrieving more material rather than by better boundaries
token-level scoring measures which tokens came back, so different chunk sizes become comparable

answers.answer: They measured different things. The negative result is scoped to sentence-level chunking, where each sentence is the segment being grouped, and reports minimal differences on its tasks and datasets rather than a loss for semantic chunking. Chroma used a different chunker (a clustering one with a maximum chunk size of 400 tokens), a different corpus, and a token-level evaluation unit. Neither result transfers to the other's setup.
accept: the negative result is limited to sentence-level chunking and to that study's datasets and tasks
the two used different chunkers, corpora, and evaluation units, including token-level scoring in one case
neither finding generalises to the other's setup, so both stand
